Learning Objectives
Identify the etiology and types of surgically and nonsurgically managed fractures that result in
nonunion.
List factors that contribute to nonunion, including patient-dependent and patient-independent
factors and the possible effect of prior surgical management on the development of nonunion.
Discuss critical biomechanical principles of fracture fixation and the manner in which they
contribute to the successful healing of a fracture or the development of a nonunion.
Describe preoperative planning and contemporary surgical treatment options for recalcitrant
nonunion.
Review effective adjuvant therapies to augment fracture healing and list levels of evidence to
support their use.

Definition of Union

Definition of Union
Union has been described in broad terms with a wide range of qualifiers, from a fracture
construct demonstrating painless weight bearing to a fracture that exhibits bridging of
three out of four cortices on orthogonal plain radiographs. Studies assessing the
reliability of radiographic assessment are limited;1,2 however, some research supports
the use of plain radiographs for assessment of long bone fractures managed via
intramedullary nailing.2
Definition of Nonunion
Nonunion is not clearly defined in the literature. Although many definitions refer to a time
after injury, a practical definition is a fracture that has no possibility of healing without
additional management, as determined by the treating surgeon.
The FDA defines a nonunion as a fractured bone that has not completely healed within 9
months post injury and shows no progression toward healing on serial radiographs obtained
over the course of 3 consecutive months.
A fracture that shows signs of progression toward healing but that is taking longer than
normal to heal is identified as a delayed union, which may require new surgical or medical
management. A difficult aspect in the management of nonunions is identifying if a fracture
requires additional management. If the healing process appears to have stopped, the fracture
may require additional management.
Epidemiology

Epidemiology
Impaired fracture healing occurs in approximately 5% to 10% of patients, a subset in
whom a fracture nonunion occurs. Nonunion rates vary substantially because of

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Nonunion occurs if the bone-healing unit fails because of mechanical and/or biologic
problems. In clinical practice, most nonunions result from mechanical problems with
instability, which causes too much strain at the fracture site.6
Multiple other contributing factors may create an environment that predisposes a fracture to
nonunion (Table 1). Each nonunion is associated with unique management problems and
challenges.

Evaluation of a patient with a nonunion requires thorough knowledge of the management of

mechanical instability, inadequate bone contact, infection, and insufficient vascularity. Any

Many factors contribute to impaired fracture healing, including the mechanical environment,
infection, metabolic abnormalities, soft-tissue compromise, patient compliance, and patient
expectations (Table 2). A well-coordinated treatment regimen that includes multispecialty
involvement must be followed.
Infection alone does not preclude fracture healing; however, it may contribute to the failure of
a fracture to progress to union. Infection should be suspected in all patients with a
nonunion.9,10

Risk Factors
Origin of Postoperative Nonunion

Origin of Postoperative Nonunion
Various biologic, mechanical, patient, and injury factors may contribute to nonunion, and
the cause of nonunion often is multifactorial. Successful management often requires
assessment and management of more than one of these factors.11,12
Improper Biomechanics
Surgical fixation of fractures may contribute to desired union; surgical fixation executed
improperly may contribute to nonunion. The combination of basic mechanical principles with
the biology of fracture healing is critical in understanding the manner in which mechanical
conditions support bony consolidation and the manner in which deviation may contribute to
nonunion.13
Strain across a fracture gap is defined as the allowed motion divided by the fracture gap. The
fracture healing pathway, intramembranous or endochondral ossification, is determined by
the amount of strain or motion across the fracture. During fracture fixation, surgeons strive to
reduce strain by controlling the stiffness or flexibility of the fixation construct. Stiff fixation
constructs that allow less than 2% strain induce intramembranous or primary bone healing;
constructs that allow 2% to 10% strain induce endochondral ossification or secondary bone
healing.
Decreasing stiffness, such that strain is greater than 30%, supports the proliferation of fibrous
tissue and results in a higher risk of nonunion (Figure 1).

Patient-dependent Factors
Various medical comorbidities, age, sex, smoking, use of NSAIDs, genetic disorders (eg,
neurofibromatosis, osteogenesis imperfecta, osteopetrosis), metabolic bone disease, and
nutritional status may contribute to fracture nonunion. Fracture healing may be inhibited by
numerous medical conditions, including diabetes mellitus and vascular disease.14,15
Medications have a substantial effect on fracture healing and may be altered after fracture to
improve healing. Because normal fracture healing is associated with inflammation and
prostaglandin synthesis, NSAIDs that interfere with these processes theoretically will interfere
with fracture healing. The inflammatory phase of fracture healing that may be inhibited is

responsible for the neovascularization and the concomitant migration of pluripotential cells
and inductive factors to the site of injury. Although this theory remains controversial, several
basic scientific and clinical studies have substantiated this hypothesis.16-18
Metabolic or endocrine pathology also may play a role in fracture healing. Undiagnosed
metabolic or endocrine pathology, including hypothyroidism or vitamin D deficiency, may
contribute to impaired fracture healing.
The nutritional status of the patient also plays a role in fracture healing.
The healing potential of chronically ill or polytrauma patients in a catabolic state is
compromised.
Patient-independent Factors
Characteristics of the injury, including the pattern of bony injury, degree of comminution,
diastasis of fracture fragments, location of the fracture, and status of the soft-tissue envelope,
may contribute to fracture nonunion. Open fractures display compromised healing secondary
to soft-tissue stripping, and an increased risk of infection is associated with these severe
injuries.
Bone loss also is a risk factor for nonunion; however, the absolute amount of bone loss
beyond which healing cannot occur has not been defined. The concept of the critical-sized
bone defect (approximately 2.5 to 3 cm of contiguous bone loss) has been introduced to
characterize an osseous defect that is not expected to heal without secondary
management.19,20
Methods of fracture management have a strong effect on fracture healing. Intraoperative
technique plays a critical role if fixation is indicated; excessive stripping of the periosteum by
the surgeon may compromise the biologic environment of the fracture and retard healing.
Inadequately stabilized fractures may not heal. Interfragmentary micromotion and low
amounts of strain stimulate intramembranous and endochondral ossification; however, a
substantial degree of strain and excessive motion at the fracture site will lead primarily to
deposition of fibrous connective tissue rather than to fracture healing. This combination of
fibrous tissue and excessive motion will lead to construct failure.

appearance (Table 3).

Hypertrophic Nonunion
Hypertrophic nonunion results from inadequate mechanical stability and exhibits surrounding
callus formation. Progressive resorption occurs at the fracture site as interposing fibrocartilage
develops with failure to mineralize. Nonunions can be categorized as elephant-foot type, with
extensive callus formation, or horse-hoof type, with a lesser degree of callus formation.
The radiographic appearance of a hypertrophic nonunion is marked by abundant callus
formation without bony bridging. This appearance indicates adequate biologic capacity for
healing but inadequate mechanical stability (Figure 3).
The primary goal of management is to provide an improved mechanical environment with
increased stability. Routine management of hypertrophic nonunion does not require opening
the fracture site or bone grafting.

Oligotrophic Nonunion
Oligotrophic nonunion result from poor bone contact in the presence of appropriate
vascularity. Radiographically, little or no callus formation is observed.
Oligotrophic nonunions exist on a continuum between and share some of the radiographic
and biologic characteristics of hypertrophic and atrophic nonunions. Typically, oligotrophic
nonunions possess adequate biologic capacity for healing but demonstrate little to no callus
formation.
Re-approximation of the bone ends and improved stability are necessary to achieve union.
Bone grafting may be performed in patients with opposing bone fragment surfaces that are
irregular and do not permit large surface-to-surface contact area. Grafting also is performed in
patients in whom a large bone fragment is missing, patients with a segmental defect, or
patients who have a fracture with questionable biologic activity.

Atrophic Nonunion
Atrophic nonunions display no callus formation and are accompanied by resorption and
osteopenia at the fracture site. In some patients with an avascular nonunion, the bone ends
surrounding the nonunion will have substantial sclerosis and lack the vascularity and
osteogenic factors necessary to stimulate osteogenesis (Figure 4).
Principles of treatment include improvement of the biologic environment and improved
mechanical stability.

A pseudarthrosis is a so-called false joint. The bone ends are atrophic with impaired
vasculature. If a pseudarthrosis is exposed surgically, the gap is filled with synovial-like tissue
with intervening fibrous connective tissue and the large void is filled with tissue exudate rather
than with true synovial fluid.
Complete surgical takedown with excision of the atrophic bone ends followed by management
according to the same principles as those for atrophic nonunions is required to effect osseous
union.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
A thorough patient history is imperative; the mechanism of injury, prior surgical and
nonsurgical management, and factors that may have contributed to a nonunion must be
identified. Essential elements of the patient history include the mechanism of injury, whether
the fracture was open or closed, the presence of pain with weight bearing, and subjective
instability.
Associated injuries and functional limitations must be identified to educate the patient on
functional expectations. Risk factors for nonunion and diagnostic tests used to assess fracture
healing may facilitate a systematic approach to evaluation and management.
Potential causes of nonunion should be investigated by examining health and nutritional
status; medical comorbidities; medications; drug, alcohol, and tobacco use; injury mechanism
and characteristics; prior management; and history of infection. History of infection or use of
antibiotic agents outside the perioperative period should be recorded.
Physicians should specifically ask about delayed wound healing, postoperative wound
drainage, and whether cellulitis was diagnosed by another physician. These issues increase
suspicion of deep infection in patients with persistent pain or compromised healing.
Physical Examination
Physical examination begins with the inspection of soft tissues to evaluate the zone of injury
for signs of infection or draining sinus tracts. The location and type of any soft-tissue transfer
should be noted.
Vascular examination is essential to evaluate for vascular insufficiency, which may contribute
to nonunion. Neurologic assessment for motor and sensory dysfunction helps identify

The limb should be evaluated for deformity, including rotational deformity and any resultant
limb-length discrepancy. Motion and pain at the nonunion site and range of motion of the
adjacent joint should be assessed. Compensatory fixed deformities at the adjacent joints must
be identified and corrected for optimal return of function.
With chronic nonunions about the knee, associated joint contracture is common.
Similarly, distal tibial nonunions often are associated with an equinus deformity of the ankle.
If the treatment plan includes bone grafting, considered donor sites must be evaluated for
prior surgical procedures or injury that may preclude graft procurement.
Imaging Studies
Conventional Radiography
Orthogonal AP, lateral, and oblique views of the affected limb are obtained to assess the
characteristics of the nonunion and limb alignment. In the lower extremities, a full-length, long
alignment weight-bearing view of both limbs from the hips to the ankles may better define
deformity and limb-length inequality. If limb-length discrepancy or deformity of the lower
extremity is a potential problem, a full-length weight-bearing view of both lower extremities is
required. Comparison views of the contralateral limb aid in preoperative planning.
Initial injury radiographs aid in assessment of the severity of the injury and account for bone
fragments that may have been removed during management. Subsequent images show
interval treatments and the progression toward the current nonunion.
Signs of nonunion include the absence of bone bridging at the fracture site, sclerotic fracture
edges, persistent fracture lines, and lack of progressive healing on serial radiographs, as well
as loosening or breakage of surgical implants. In patients in whom fixation fails, the fracture
site should be scrutinized for technical adequacy. The surgeon should assess for a callus
response that is appropriate relative to the construct type.
Radiographic Union Scale for Tibial Fractures: This scale was developed by Whelan et al21 to
assess the healing of tibial fractures after intramedullary nailing. It is a reliable and repeatable
outcome measure for assessing tibial fracture healing. Its application to other long bone
anatomic sites is evolving (Table 4).
If anatomic reduction and interfragmentary compression are achieved, primary bone healing
without fracture callus should be expected. If nonsurgical management or less stable fixation
has been used, secondary bone healing with callus formation should be observed.

Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography can be performed to detect hyperechoic fracture callus.
Despite the advantages of earlier detection of union and avoidance of ionizing radiation,
ultrasonography is user dependent and not routinely used to assess fracture healing.
Computed Tomography
A CT scan may provide additional detail on union and articular injury or malreduction.
Sclerotic bone and surrounding hardware often obscure the fracture site on plain radiographs.
Quality may be limited by the presence of metallic implants.
Although the high sensitivity associated with CT suggests that it may be effective as an initial
screening modality in patients with equivocal tibial fracture healing, CT is limited by a low
specificity that may generate false-positive results, leading to unnecessary surgical
management.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI has some diagnostic benefit in the workup for a potentially infected nonunion.
This imaging modality can be performed to assess the presence and extent of pathologic
changes in the bone marrow and surrounding soft tissues.
Laboratory Studies
A workup to screen for infection must be performed, including a complete blood count with
differential, platelet count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. The
presence of normal inflammatory markers does not exclude the possibility of infection at the
nonunion site.22
An endocrine evaluation also should be considered for apparently healthy patients with a
nonunion who have undergone technically appropriate and uncomplicated treatment.
Laboratory tests evaluating endocrine abnormalities include calcium, vitamin D, parathyroid
hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and testosterone levels (Figure 6).
Nutritional laboratory tests to consider include albumin level, prealbumin level, and absolute
lymphocyte count.2
Initial laboratory screening, including tests to assess serum calcium, serum 25-hydroxyvitamin
D, thyroid-stimulating hormone, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase levels, can be ordered
by the orthopaedic surgeon.

Needle Aspiration and Biopsy
A needle aspiration or biopsy specimen can be obtained from the nonunion site for culture
and histologic evaluation. In some scenarios, these may be the best methods to determine
infection status. The surgeon can pursue needle aspiration or biopsy as a staged
reconstructive effort before definitive revision surgery. Alternatively, the surgeon can await
Gram stain and the number of white blood cells per high power field during the index
procedure; however, this may be variable.24,25
Sonication
Sonication involves the use of high-frequency sound waves to mechanically dislodge adherent
bacteria from the biofilm. By exposing the explanted prosthesis to sound wave impulses in a
saline bath, the adherent bacteria-laden biofilm is disrupted, resulting in an increased
bacterial yield on culture media.
Previous studies have found that cultures derived from sonication is a simple, inexpensive,
and clinically useful method for the detection of implant-associated infections on prostheses,

Management
General Indications, Goals, and Obstacles
Indications for nonunion management include failure to improve clinically, such as continued
severe pain and inability to bear weight, and lack of radiographic progression of fracture
healing, such as the absence of bridging bone observed on plain radiographs or CT scans for 2
or more consecutive months after fracture.
The goal of management is to heal the non-united fracture and regain function of the
extremity. Management is designed with an understanding of physical and psychologic
components of the condition.
A systematic approach that involves a multidisciplinary team often is necessary for successful
outcomes in patients with a complex nonunion. A systematic approach is required to identify
and manage any biologic issues and to address the mechanical environment.
Nonunion management requires thorough knowledge of the etiology of a nonunion and the
various treatment options. Each nonunion is unique and associated with its own challenges
because of the variability in nonunion type, injury characteristics, prior management, patient
comorbidities, and treatment options.
Factors that contribute to the formation of nonunion include biologic, mechanical, patient, and
injury factors; however, frequently, the cause of nonunion is multifactorial. Successful
management often requires that multiple factors be addressed concurrently.
Stable fixation with optimization of nonunion surface characteristics, mechanical stability, and
the biologic environment is key to the management of nonunion.
Preoperative Characterization of Nonunion
Biologic capacity
A hypertrophic appearance indicates adequate biologic capacity and a likelihood of healing
via stabilization alone.

Atrophic appearance indicates inadequate biologic capacity, and the addition of an
osteoinductive or osteogenic agent generally is required for healing.
Oligotrophic nonunions share some characteristics with hypertrophic and atrophic
nonunions; these nonunions typically possess adequate biologic capacity for healing but
demonstrate little to no callus formation.
Deformity
Length, alignment, and rotation must be evaluated.
Limb lengths of the injured and contralateral extremity should be determined. Full-length
standing AP radiographs of the lower extremities or a single-cut CT scan is effective for this
comparison.
Rotational deformities may be difficult to characterize, and a CT scan of the affected and
contralateral extremity may aid in comparison.
Most tibial nonunions with deformity usually are associated with rotational malalignment.
Infection
Determining whether a nonunion is infected is a critical step in formulating an appropriate
treatment plan.
After obtaining a thorough initial patient history, performing a physical examination, and
performing a complete radiographic and laboratory evaluation, the surgeon must determine
if an indolent infection is suspected.
Needle aspiration or biopsy can be performed if uncertainty persists. If no collection can be
detected, then open biopsy can be performed in the operating room. To maximize the
likelihood of identifying an organism, antibiotic agents should be discontinued 2 weeks
before open biopsy. Biopsy specimens should be submitted for Gram stain, cell count,
culture, and pathology. Multiple specimens should be obtained.

Nonsurgical Management
Indications

Indications
Nonsurgical treatment is a viable option for a small percentage of patients because
some nonunions may be asymptomatic (eg, base of the fifth metatarsal, medial
malleolus) and the patient may accept the current ununited status and function.
Contraindications

Contraindications
In some patients, particularly those with an upper extremity nonunion and elderly
patients with sufficient function and minimal pain, surgical treatment may result in
greater morbidity than leaving the nonunion unmanaged.
Techniques/Procedures
Fracture brace immobilization with axial loading of the limb is a viable treatment option for
certain rigid/stable nonunions.
Bone growth stimulators (inductive or capacitive coupling devices) are an option for some
patients. High-level evidence is unavailable. Accepted contraindications to electrical

Surgical Management
Indications
After diagnosis of a nonunion, knowledge of the etiology is the first step in creating a
treatment regimen. Infected, hypertrophic, oligotrophic, and atrophic nonunions and
nonunions associated with segmental defects require specific treatment approaches.
Fortification of the mechanical environment is a treatment concept shared by all nonunion
types29 (Resource 3).
The goal in the surgical management of nonunions is to create a favorable environment for
fracture healing. Necessary factors include stable fixation and a biologically viable
environment.29
Mechanical and biologic factors contribute to nonunions. Based on these observations,
Andrzejowski and Giannoudis30 introduced the so-called diamond concept for successful bone
healing, which emphasizes the effect of the mechanical environment, osteogenic cells,
scaffolds, and growth factors (Figure 7).

Mechanics of Fracture Fixation Failure
To promote union in a new fracture, the treating surgeon must select the proper desired
biomechanical stability pathway (absolute versus relative) for osseous union and a fixation
implant and method of insertion (indirect versus direct reduction) that will contribute to a
successful outcome. Deviation from these principles may result in a fracture site nonunion.
Fixation-induced strain may contribute to nonunion. The amount of strain depends on fracture
comminution, the size of the fracture gap, and the overall stability of the construct. Basic
principles of fracture fixation assert that comminuted fractures respond well to bridge plating
and relative stability, whereas simple fractures should be anatomically reduced, compressed,
and stabilized rigidly.
Stress modulation is the concept of manipulating plate fixation variables to provide a flexible
fixation construct that allows for callus formation via uneventful secondary bone healing.
Improper stress modulation may result in nonunion and generate an undesirable outcome.
Stress modulation concepts also are applicable to intramedullary nails and external fixators as
well31 (Resource 4).

The same tenets associated with primary fixation efforts must be respected and adhered to in

Plate Fixation Concerns
Plate fixation for nonunion involves various techniques to improve stability at the nonunion
site, including compression, bridge, locking, dual, wave, and augmentative plating.
Direct exposure of the nonunion site during plating procedures allows the surgeon to débride
the nonunion site if necessary, such as for infected nonunions, atrophic nonunions, and select
oligotrophic nonunions.
Disadvantages that may limit plate use include wide surgical dissection, limited–weight bearing
postoperatively, and the static nature of fixation.
Comminuted periarticular fractures are a challenge to manage because they typically require
absolute stability across the articular segment for primary bone healing and flexible fixation
across areas of metadiaphyseal comminution for secondary bone healing. Absolute stability at
the articular surface and relative stability across the metadiaphysis is a common fixation
schema, resulting in intramembranous and enchondral ossifications, respectively.
Promoting different healing modalities in the same bone necessitates that the fixation
constructs provide different mechanical properties. One of the most common fractures that
requires a combination of healing modalities is a distal femur fracture. An increasing body of

Intramedullary Nailing Fixation Concerns
Management of long bone nonunions via intramedullary nailing is optimal in many patients
because of its mechanical strength and load-sharing capabilities. This is especially important in
patients with a lower extremity nonunion.

because of the potential for intramedullary sepsis.
Exchange nailing has been shown to be a successful technique for the successful management
of lower extremity long bone nonunions. Various techniques of compression nailing also have
been described for the management of nonunion (Figure 9).

metadiaphyseal region via intramedullary nailing. Increasing the stability of these fractures has
been attempted by increasing nail size (reaming), which is a well-established practice, and via

An example of augmentation plating is the application of a plate (supplementation) to a
fracture that was previously managed via an intramedullary nail in which the fracture

Locked plating constructs provide inherently rigid stabilization; however, they facilitate biologic
fixation and secondary bone healing that relies on flexible fixation to stimulate callus

constructs may suppress interfragmentary motion to a level that is insufficient to reliably
promote secondary fracture healing via callus formation.41-43

are fixed in the plate and in the far cortex while retaining a controlled motion envelope in the

The technique of distraction osteogenesis has been used to manage effectively traumatic
skeletal defects. Originally, Ilizarov and others stabilized the limb with the use of a circular
external fixator, and the bone transport segment was produced via osteotomy of the
metaphysis. After a 5-day latent period, this segment is transported approximately 1 mm/d to
eliminate the diaphyseal segmental bone defect and create a new defect at the osteotomy site.
This defect fills with new bone via distraction osteogenesis. The docking site heals in
compression v fracture callus. For each day of distraction, 2 to 3 days of consolidation are
required. Bone graft typically is applied to the docking site, and the ends of the bone may be
freshened to stimulate healing (Figure 20).
Traditional internal bone transport has been successfully used for bony reconstruction for
acute and reconstructive bone loss. Potential complications are primarily related to the
complexity of the external device, prolonged time in the frame, and nonunion of the docking
and regeneration segments. Recent advances in fixator and pin design have reduced the
complexity of these devices and the incidence of pin- and frame-related complications.
Gradual shortening, rapid distraction via auto distractors, transporting over intramedullary
devices, and using orthobiologic and adjuvant techniques to aid in the consolidation of
regeneration and docking sites currently are being combined to decrease the morbidity and

some specific femoral nonunions. The indications for plating osteosynthesis (to manage
femoral diaphyseal nonunions) include hypertrophic nonunions and proximal and distal
metadiaphyseal nonunions in which intramedullary nailing may be difficult. In oligotrophic or

Circular external fixators (Ilizarov-type fixators) also have been used for the management of
femoral nonunions. The principal role of this type of fixation mainly involves the management
of infected nonunions. The role of circular external fixators is limited in aseptic nonunions.169
Distal Femur Nonunion
The most common reported risk factor is an open fracture. Proper so-called screw balance
(more empty holes adjacent to the fracture) appears beneficial for healing and callous
formation compared with fractures that do not ultimately heal.170-172
Although locking plates are a valuable additional option for the management of distal femur
fractures, complications related to slow healing, including nonunion, delayed union, and
implant failure, are not infrequent. With locking plate fixation, callus forms disproportionately
at the medial cortex opposite the plate compared with the anterior and posterior cortices.173
Less callus also is formed in fractures managed via stainless steel plates compared with those
managed via more flexible titanium plates. The stiffer nature of the stainless plates may
contribute to increased nonunion rates.
Revising an initial locking plate (alone) for the definitive management of distal femur
nonunions is associated with mixed results. The main principles in the management a distal
femur nonunion are improved reduction, correction of the medial bone defect, and biologic
support via bone grafting.
From a mechanical perspective, the application of a medial strut graft or a medial column plate
may be useful in the management of these nonunions. The addition of bone graft, staged
reconstruction, and revision of the initial lateral plate are indicated if the nonunion is
associated with fatigue failure of the initial lateral plate174,175 (Figure 27).
Evidence supports favorable outcomes with the use of double (medial and lateral) plating for
the management of distal femoral fractures, periprosthetic fractures, and distal femur
nonunions. Combined nail/plate constructs with the inclusion of autogenous bone grafting
also are associated with considerable success.176,177

Four-compartment fasciotomies in patients with a tibial shaft or plateau fracture are
associated with a marked increase in infection and nonunion.189
A so-called critical-sized defect is defined as a defect that is not expected to heal in the
absence of secondary management. A critical-sized tibial defect involves 50% of the cortical
diameter of the tibia and has a length of 1 cm. These criteria have been increasingly
challenged.190,191
Distal Tibia Nonunion
Bone loss, open fracture, failure to manage the medial column, locking plates, and tobacco use
are notable risk factors for tibial plafond nonunion. Surgical approach selection may not be
closely associated with plafond nonunion192,193 (Figure 28).
Fibular fixation may improve achievement and maintenance of reduction in patients with a
complex fracture of the distal tibia; however, because of the increased stability of the
construct, it also may increase the risk of nonunion.184,194,195
The inclusion of posterolateral bone grafting to manage distal nonunions is associated with
successful outcomes.196
